agent_notes: The title עַלְמוּת לַבֵּן is of unknown meaning. I kept 'alumoth labben' in the literal layer instead of choosing among the readings the commentators offer (Rashi/Ibn Ezra/Radak: 'on the death of Laban/the son', a tune, a person named Ben, Goliath 'the man between', Nabal reversed). The Masoretic pointing is one word, עַלְמוּת, as in Ps 48:15; the KJV 'Muth-labben' follows the split עַל־מוּת. STEPBible glosses 'alumoth' and 'labben' as names; I glossed them as transliterations with the traditional readings in the notes.

In the packet the verse map puts this title as KJV 9:0, so every later verse is KJV n-1 (PS.9.2 = KJV 9:1). I translated the Hebrew verses as they stand. The Rashi quotation about 'purified youth' (הכתוב עלמות ... כשיתלבן) is a midrashic reading; I cite it only as a reading, not as the sense.

agent_notes: STEPBible glosses דַּךְ as 'oppressed'. The word is 'crushed' (from דכא, Rashi cites Ps 90:3 דַּכָּא); I used 'the crushed' in the literal layer. The Masoretic form of 'in trouble' is בַּצָּרָה, a single word which the KJV reads as 'in times of trouble' by taking בְּ with צָרָה.

agent_notes: 'Hanneni' is a prayer imperative; the five English versions all say 'have mercy'. I used 'show me favor' in the literal layer to keep the root chanan (grace). The participle 'meromemi' (one lifting me) is vocative-like; KJV, ASV and Webster make it a relative clause ('thou that liftest me up'), BBE turns it into a wish. I kept it as an address to YHWH.

agent_notes: Disputed: 'noqesh' is a Niphal participle of yaqosh (to be snared) in Radak and Meiri; Ibn Ezra and Radak's alternative see a root nqsh. I translate 'snared' in both layers. 'Higgaion' and 'Selah' are kept as untranslated markers in the literal layer; the dramatic layer keeps only a pause. The meaning of both terms is uncertain and I do not claim a certain one.

'lish'olah' carries a directional he as well as the lamed (to Sheol-ward). Rashi and Radak cite the Talmudic reading (Yevamot 13b, Sanhedrin 105a, as the commentaries give it) that the doubling points to the lowest level of Sheol or Gehinnom. I report this as a tradition; it is not in the plain sense of the verse. 'yashuvu' is imperfect; the commentaries disagree whether it is a prediction or a wish (Radak: a prayer); I translate it as a plain future.

Reviewer request addressed: the 'as in 9.13' remark is replaced by a note that the Ketiv/Qere pair here is the reverse of 9:13. Here the written form is ענוים ('anavim, 'humble') and the read form is עניים ('aniyyim, 'afflicted'); at 9:13 it is written עניים and read ענוים (Radak on Psalms 9:13 and 9:19, as quoted in the packet). The packet's word table shows only the Qere, with the transliteration 'anavim' that belongs to the Ketiv; I glossed the reading and named the written form in the note. I did not check the Ketiv/Qere of 9:13 against the manuscript, only Radak's report of it.

Radak (and Metzudat David) explain that the single 'not' (לֹא) of the first line also governs 'will be lost' in the second, so the line reads 'not ... will be lost'. I followed that in the literal layer by letting the first 'not' carry over, without adding a second one.

agent_notes: Reviewer request addressed: the predicate is now given first, as in the Hebrew: 'enosh hemmah', 'human [are] they'. The STEPBible gloss '[are] human being[s]' for אֱנוֹשׁ is kept in spirit; the word is a noun used as predicate, with no verb in the Hebrew.

מוֹרָה is disputed. Ibn Ezra, Radak and Meiri read it as a spelling of מוֹרָא 'fear' (ה for א), which is what KJV, ASV, BBE and Webster follow ('put them in fear'). Rashi and Metzudat Zion give 'throwing/casting' (as in יָרָה, Exodus 15:4), and Rashi also 'mastery, yoke'. YLT has 'a director' (from the root ירה 'teach', as in מוֹרֶה). I chose 'fear' for both layers, since it is the majority reading and fits 'let the nations know that they are human'; the alternatives are in the commentary. The packet's STEPBible gloss 'terror' agrees.
סֶלָה is left untranslated in all layers; Ibn Ezra's gloss 'truly' (באמת) is quoted as one traditional guess and not adopted. The word-gloss for it is 'Selah'.

agent_notes: A famously difficult verse. Syntax of הָאוֹיֵב is disputed: a vocative (Radak, Meiri: ה of address, as in Num 15:15 and Jer 2:31) or a collective subject. Also disputed is whose 'ruins' and whose 'memory' are meant (the enemy's own cities, or the cities the enemy destroyed). I followed the vocative reading with the ruins as the ruins the enemy made and the cities as the cities he uprooted; the dramatic layer stays close to that. Ibn Ezra's alternate reading (with a punctuated וְעָרִים נָתַשְׁתָּ as a separate clause) is also reasonable. The final הֵמָּה ('they', even them) is left as a closing emphatic and I did not try to resolve whether it is rhetorical question (Radak's second reading).

STEPBible glosses כּוֹנֵן as a perfect 'he has established'; the form is a polel perfect 3ms (or participle with unusual pointing). I kept the perfect in the literal layer. ASV/Webster's 'sitteth as king' vs. KJV 'endure' both reflect the sense of יֵשֵׁב; the literal layer keeps 'sits'.
